propositions.text: The claimant and her children are Croatian citizens claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: The claimant XXXX XXXX (hereafter the claimant), and her children, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX are citizens of Croatia, and are claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

propositions.text: The claimant was made Designated Representative for her minor dependants.
propositions.quote: The claimant was made Designated Representative for her minor dependants, XXXX and XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant and her children are Croatian citizens claiming refugee protection and that the claimant is their Designated Representative.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges she is a 53-year-old woman born in Serbia, moved to Serbia at age four, married, lived there 18 years, had two children, and the marriage was abusive.
propositions.quote: She alleged that she is a 53 year old woman who was born in XXXX, Serbia. She alleged that her parents moved to Serbia when she was four years old. The claimant returned to Serbia, was married, and lived in XXXX XXXX for eighteen years. She has two children from that union, XXXX and XXXX. The claimant alleged that the marriage was abusive.

propositions.text: In 1992, she moved to Croatia with her children, began a common-law relationship, had four children, and married in 2000, resulting in Croatian citizenship only.
propositions.quote: In 1992, she moved with her children to XXXX, Croatia. The claimant alleged that she met XXXX XXXX. In XXXX of that same year, they began a common-law relationship. The union produced four children. The claimant alleged that she was considered a foreign citizen in Croatia because her parents did not register her as a Croatian citizen and she had to renounce her Serbian citizenship in order to marry XXXX XXXX. She alleged that she married him on XXXX XXXX, 2000. As a result, she only has Croatian citizenship.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges her background, abusive first marriage, move to Croatia, common-law relationship, marriage, and Croatian citizenship.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges her husband became abusive around 2006, beat children, police ignored complaints due to Roma ethnicity, and husband breached restraining order.
propositions.quote: She alleged he became very abusive and accused her of being unfaithful. She alleged that he would beat their children. The claimant also alleged that on many occasions she called the police, but the police did not care much because she and her family were just worthless Roma. She alleged that, in 2010, her husband was arrested as a result of his behaviour towards his family. Upon his release, he was issued a restraining order which prohibited him from coming within 300 meters of their residence. The claimant alleged that her husband however moved to their neighbour's home, which was located about 30 meters from their family home, and continued to harass her regularly. She alleged that she reported the breach to the authorities and he was fined 2,700 Kunas. However, she alleged that he was not compelled to leave the area.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges her husband became abusive, police ignored complaints due to Roma ethnicity, and husband breached restraining order.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges her husband raped her daughter in 2011, was arrested but only fined, and continued to attack her after she moved out.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that her husband raped her daughter. She alleged that he was arrested, but later released with only a fine. The claimant then moved out with her children and went to live at XXXX home in XXXX XXXX, but her husband came there and attacked her and bit her on one of her ears.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges police arrested husband after attack, she was treated at hospital, moved back home, filed for divorce finalized in 2010, but husband continued to beat her.
propositions.quote: The police were called and he was arrested. The claimant was treated at hospital, but she alleged that on XXXX XXXX, she moved back to her home in XXXX. The claimant however alleged that she filed for divorce; the divorce was finalized on XXXX XXXX, 2010. But, her husband was still coming to the home and beating her.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges her husband raped her daughter, was fined, attacked her, and continued abuse despite divorce.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges she found ex-husband assaulting daughter, police were unhelpful and dismissive about 'Gypsy matters'.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that one day she returned home and found her ex-husband on top of XXXX while their other daughter, XXXX was screaming. She called the police, but was told by the police that they were fed up with their Gypsy matters.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges police were dismissive when she reported ex-husband assaulting daughter.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges ex-husband was arrested in 2011, jailed three months, but resumed harassment after release; family left Croatia and filed refugee claim in Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that on XXXX 2011 her ex-husband was arrested and he spent three months in jail, but on his release he returned to harassing and beating the claimant. He was arrested again and held until XXXX XXXX, 2011. The claimant alleged that while he was in prison she and her children left Croatia and came to Canada. On October 28, 2011 the claimant and her children filed for refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges ex-husband jailed in 2011 but resumed abuse; family fled to Canada and filed refugee claim.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimant has not established serious possibility of persecution or risk of torture, death, or cruel treatment upon return.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant has not established that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities she would personally be subjected to a danger of torture, or face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment, or punishment upon return to her country.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant failed to establish serious persecution or risk upon return.

propositions.text: The determinative issues are credibility and state protection.
propositions.quote: The determinative issues in this case are credibility and state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The panel identifies credibility and state protection as key issues.

propositions.text: The panel is satisfied claimants are Croatian citizens based on testimony and passport documents.
propositions.quote: The panel is satisfied that the claimants are citizens of Croatia based on the claimant's testimony and the supporting documentation filed including her personal identity based on certified true copies of their Croatian passports.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants are Croatian citizens based on evidence.

propositions.text: The Chairperson's Gender Guidelines were considered, including social and cultural context and hearing sensitivities.
propositions.quote: The Chairperson's Gender Guidelines3 were taken into account when considering the process of the hearing and the facts in this case. All relevant factors, such as the social and cultural context in which the claimant found herself, were considered pursuant to the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.

propositions.text: The panel took into account difficulties faced by claimant including cultural factors and stress in hearing, applying heightened sensitivity and avoiding unnecessary detail.
propositions.quote: Given the sensitive nature of the allegations, the panel is cognizant of the difficulties faced by the claimant in establishing her claim including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter. The panel has taken these considerations into account in arriving at its finding of negative credibility. The panel addressed the claimant with heightened sensitivity and avoided unnecessary detail when asking questions about sensitive issues.

paragraphs.summary: The panel applied Gender Guidelines and sensitivity due to cultural and hearing stress factors.

propositions.text: The panel finds adequate state protection exists in Croatia and claimant failed to prove lack of protection with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, the panel finds that adequate state protection exists for individuals like the claimant in Croatia. Based on the totality of evidence adduced, the panel finds that Croatian authorities are making serious efforts to provide adequate protection at the operational level to individuals like the claimant. The panel finds that the claimant has not met the burden of establishing clear and convincing evidence of lack of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds Croatia provides adequate state protection and claimant failed to prove otherwise.

propositions.text: Claimant must prove state protection is inadequate on balance of probabilities with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate. To rebut the presumption of state protection the claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

propositions.text: Evidence of inadequate state protection must be reliable, probative, and satisfy balance of probabilities standard.
propositions.quote: The evidence that state protection is inadequate, must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: No government guarantees perfect protection; failure to protect all citizens is insufficient for claim if state controls territory and makes serious protection efforts.
propositions.quote: Unfortunately, no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state has control of its territories, has military, police, and civil authorities in place and is making a serious effort to protect its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The panel explains the legal standard for proving inadequate state protection and the presumption of state protection.

propositions.text: States are presumed capable of protecting citizens unless state is in complete breakdown.
propositions.quote: The courts have found that states are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in the case of state that is in complete breakdown.

propositions.text: Croatia is a functioning democracy with EU membership and a security apparatus capable of protecting citizens.
propositions.quote: Croatia is a state which entered the European Union, and as such had to address its human rights conditions, its judiciary, its security, and all aspects of its governance to meet the standards of the European Union. The presumption then is that the state is capable of protecting its citizens. Having reviewed the National Documentation Package and documents from the claimant, the panel finds that Croatia is a democracy in control of its territory and has a functioning security apparatus to uphold its laws and its constitution.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds Croatia is a functioning democracy presumed capable of protecting citizens.

propositions.text: Croatia is a constitutional parliamentary democracy with legislative, executive, and security forces under civilian control; elections meet international standards.
propositions.quote: The Republic of Croatia is a constitutional parliamentary democracy. Legislative authority is vested in the unicameral parliament (the Sabor). The president serves as head of state and nominates the prime minister, who leads the government. Domestic and international observers stated that parliamentary elections held in December were in accordance with international standards. Security forces reported to civilian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The panel describes Croatia's democratic government and civilian-controlled security forces.

propositions.text: Croatia has functioning security and judicial systems with rights to public trial, counsel, and appeal; recent legal aid law amendments may not improve access significantly.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that Croatia has a functioning security apparatus and judicial processes, which have removed barriers to accessing assistance from the legal community. "The national police have primary responsibility for domestic national security. However, in times of disorder, the prime minister and the president may call upon the military to provide security. The intelligence service is under the authority of the prime minister and the president. An independent oversight board monitors the intelligence service's activity." "The constitution and law provide for the right to a public trial, and an independent judiciary generally enforced this right. Defendants enjoy the presumption of innocence. To hear cases, the legal system uses panels of judges that in some cases include lay judges, rather than juries. Defendants have the right to counsel, to be present at trial, to confront or question witnesses against them, and to present witnesses and evidence on their behalf. Defendants have access to evidence relevant to their cases and have the right to appeal." "On April 6, the Constitutional Court annulled five articles of the law on free legal aid due to restrictive and vague provisions that hindered vulnerable individuals from accessing free legal aid. On July 14, the amended law addressing the Constitutional Court's requirements took effect. However, a group of 30 NGOs, including the umbrella NGO Human Rights House, the ombudsman, and legal experts from the Zagreb Law School, doubted that the new legislation would significantly improve the referral system or make legal aid more accessible."

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds Croatia has functioning security and judicial systems with some concerns about legal aid access.

propositions.text: The burden on claimant to prove lack of state protection increases with the democracy level of the state.
propositions.quote: When the state in question is a democratic state, the way the burden of proof rests on the claimant is directly proportional to the level of the democracy of the state in question; the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to him or her.

propositions.text: Refugee protection is surrogate, invoked only when claimant unsuccessfully sought home state protection.
propositions.quote: Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state.

propositions.text: Claimant must show she sought but failed to obtain home state protection or that state could not be expected to provide protection.
propositions.quote: To qualify for refugee status, a claimant must satisfy the Board that she has sought, but was unable to obtain, protection from her home state, or alternatively, that her home state, on an objective basis, could not be expected to provide protection.

propositions.text: Failure to pursue state protection usually fatal to claim, especially in functioning democracies with protection apparatus.
propositions.quote: In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the claimant's home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, especially where the state is a functioning democracy with willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.

propositions.text: Testimony under oath is presumed true unless valid reason to doubt.
propositions.quote: The panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal, which has ruled that testimony given under oath is presumed to be true, unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe claimant was persecuted by husband since 2006 and that she manipulated facts about domestic violence and Roma discrimination to claim lack of state protection.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe that the claimant was a victim of persecution in her country because she was victimized by her husband since 2006 and despite making complaints to the authorities received no protection. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has used a basic set of facts, specifically that domestic violence is a problem in Croatia and that Roma face widespread discrimination, and through manipulation of those facts, the claimant has concocted a story that she did not receive adequate state protection in her country.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence claimant called police many times between 2006-2010 and police were indifferent.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that on many occasions she called the police, but they did not care much. However, there is no persuasive evidence before this panel that the claimant called the police on 'many occasions' between 2006 and 2010 and that they were indifferent to her calls.

propositions.text: Counsel argued claimant provided evidence of past incidents where state protection failed despite efforts, including police refusal and ethnic discrimination.
propositions.quote: Counsel in his submissions stated that the claimant "provided evidence of past incidents in which state protection failed to materialize in spite of efforts to engage such protection". He also added that "Ms. XXXX explained how police refused to assist her when she attempted to obtain help in regard to domestic violence, and that, instead of being offered protection, she was at times called derogatory names linked to her Roma ethnicity".

propositions.text: Counsel cited documentary evidence of police indifference to domestic violence and Roma discrimination to support claimant's lack of state protection claim.
propositions.quote: In addition, counsel in his written submissions cited several pieces of documentary evidence about police indifference to complaints made both by victims of domestic violence and instances of discrimination against Roma in order to suggest that the claimant's story of a lack of state protection is credible and sho

paragraphs.summary: The panel explains burden of proof for state protection, finds claimant manipulated facts, and notes counsel's arguments about police indifference and discrimination.

propositions.text: The panel disagrees with counsel that claimant lacked adequate state protection and notes no persuasive evidence of domestic violence before 2010.
propositions.quote: The panel disagrees with counsel that the claimant did not obtain adequate state protection and in doing so reminds itself that it is not sufficient to rely solely on documentary evidence listing certain flaws or weaknesses in the country's justice system. As the panel noted before, there is no persuasive evidence before it, that the claimant was a victim of domestic violence prior to 2010.

propositions.text: Counsel argued police only acted in 2010 due to social services involvement and claimant's earlier pleas were ignored.
propositions.quote: Counsel makes the point, speculatively as it may be, that "Although Ms. XXXX was able to attain police involvement in her situation in 2010 and 2011, it appears that it was only because of the involvement of a social services agency that the police decided to address the matter in 2010. For many years prior to 2010 Ms. XXXX plea for assistance from the police were ignored" .

propositions.text: If claimant sought police help before 2010, she would have received help similar to 2010; no evidence social services only existed after 2010 or no help was available before then.
propositions.quote: If the claimant was a victim of domestic violence prior to 2010 and had sought help from the police, as the claimant said she did, on a balance of probabilities, she would have received help in much the same way she received help in 2010 and after. For example, there is no evidence before this panel that the social services agency which counsel alluded to in his submissions only came into existence in 2010. Or that prior to 2010 there was not any help available for victims of domestic violence.

propositions.text: The Government adopted the Law on Protection against Domestic Violence in 2003; Centers for Social Welfare offer mandated free counseling and protective services.
propositions.quote: The panel notes that "In 2003, the Government adopted the Law on Protection against Domestic Violence (LPDV)". Centers for Social Welfare (CSWs), which counsel alluded to "as social services agency" are mandated to offer free counselling services, among a variety of other services. Their role is to protect and prevent domestic violence.

propositions.text: CSWs are mandated under LPDV and Family Law to offer various measures to victims, including referrals, financial assistance, treatment programs, court recommendations, and investigations.
propositions.quote: CSWs are mandated under the LPDV and the Family Law to offer a wide range of measures to victims. Such services may include referrals to shelters, awarding victims one-off financial assistance, requiring victims, perpetrators and children to attend treatment programmes, making recommendations to the courts for perpetrator punishment, and making recommendations for the custody of children. In addition, CSWs must comply with mandatory reporting requirements and conduct investigations.

propositions.text: CSWs act as gatekeepers for shelters; victims must register with CSW to access publicly funded shelters; counsel acknowledged CSW involvement.
propositions.quote: They also act as gatekeepers between victims and shelter, and even if they have gone to the police, victims are required to register with the CSW to be placed in publicly-run or -funded shelters. Counsel is on record for acknowledging that a CSW got involved.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds no evidence of domestic violence before 2010, notes legal protections and social services existed, and rejects counsel's argument about police inaction before 2010.

propositions.text: The panel finds a 2010 physical and verbal altercation involving claimant's husband and nephew, followed by assault on claimant and daughter, leading to husband's arrest, conviction, and sentencing.
propositions.quote: The panel believes that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 the claimant's husband and his nephew, XXXX XXXX were involved in a physical and verbal altercation for which they were both charged by the police. Later that evening the claimant was also physically and verbally assaulted by her husband. The claimant's husband also verbally assaulted their daughter XXXX. As a consequence, the claimant's husband was arrested, charged, tried, convicted in a court of law on four counts, and sentenced (1st count) 15 days, (2nd count) fined 730.00 kuna, (3rd count) 30 days, and (4th count) 45 days, for a total of 90 days imprisonment.

propositions.text: The panel finds this was the first physical violence incident between claimant and husband, though heated arguments occurred before.
propositions.quote: The panel believes this was the first instance of physical violence between the claimant and her husband. But the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant and her husband had engaged in heated arguments in the past.

propositions.text: Court record indicates children were frightened as arguments were not first time, suggesting prior verbal disputes.
propositions.quote: For example, as the court record indicated, the children "got frightened due to the fact that this was not the first time that they argued between them". This suggests to the panel that the claimant and her husband would argue before the children.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds a 2010 assault incident leading to husband's conviction and that prior to this only verbal disputes occurred.

propositions.text: No mention of prior physical violence; if existed, would likely be mentioned like prior arguments.
propositions.quote: As the panel notes, there is no mention of any previous physical violence and finds that if there was any previous instance of physical violence, on a balance of probabilities it would have been mentioned just like how it was mentioned that it was not the first time they argued between themselves.

propositions.text: The 2010 physical violence incident was reported and led to police action, divorce proceedings, and involvement of Centers for Social Welfare.
propositions.quote: This incident of physical violence, as it should be, was enough for the claimant. Divorce proceedings were commenced. She wrote "I had filed for divorce in the year 2010, which was finalized on XXXX XXXX, 2010". The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that because physical violence, for the first time, was now introduced into the equation in XXXX 2010, the incident was reported to the authorities, and action was taken. In addition, because the violence was now reported and the divorce proceedings had commenced, and especially since children were also involved, the CSW also got involved in accordance with the LPDV.

propositions.text: Family Law requires mediation in divorce; police involvement preceded CSW involvement; CSW reports cover 2010-2012; claimant reported husband's long-term threats and abuse to CSW.
propositions.quote: For example, according to documentary evidence, The Family Law requires married couples (and their children) going through divorce proceedings to complete mediation as part of the divorce process. Thus, the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the police did not get involved in the case of domestic violence merely because the CSW was involved. In fact, they were involved before the CSW. For example, the CSW report indicate "starting from XXXX XXXX XXXX.2010 to XXXX XXXX XXXX.2012", while the judgment of the court became effective on XXXX XXXX, 2010. At any rate, the important thing is that the police, when the matter came to their attention, took action. The panel however notes that the claimant advised the CSW that her husband "several years back, almost on a daily basis threatens conducts toward his wife and children psychological and physical mistreatment, consumes alcohol and then utters towards wife and children physical threats".

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds no prior physical violence, that 2010 violence led to police and CSW involvement, and notes claimant's reports of long-term threats.

propositions.text: Counsel admitted claimant received some police assistance leading to husband's charges and incarceration.
propositions.quote: Counsel, however, admitted that the claimant received protection, even if she did so reluctantly. For example, she submitted that "police provided some assistance" to Ms. XXXX which led to her abusive spouse's charges, conviction, and incarceration.

propositions.text: Counsel argued state protection is rebutted due to past failures, police failure to enforce orders, and country condition documents.
propositions.quote: But she added that because of her (a) past experience and efforts to seek state protection on many occasions did not materialize, and the fact that the (2) police failed to enforce court orders and the (3) country condition documents, state protection is rebutted.

propositions.text: Counsel cited claimant's testimony that police routinely violated court orders and failed to act on breaches despite reports.
propositions.quote: Counsel pointed to the claimant's testimony, she "testified how her former spouse routinely violated Court orders which imposed no-contact provisions" and that the "police failed to act to enforce the Court Orders or charge her former spouse upon breaches, although Ms. XXXX reported the breaches to the police".

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant's allegations of police failure to enforce orders unsupported by documentary evidence and prefers documentary evidence over claimant's testimony.
propositions.quote: But the claimant's allegation that her husband breached court orders and that the police failed to respond to her complaints is not supported by the documentary evidence she provided. The panel prefers the documentary evidence over the claimant's testimony since they are drawn from a wide range of publicly accessible documents from reliable non-government and government organizations.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel admits some police assistance but argues state protection failed; panel finds claimant's allegations unsupported and prefers documentary evidence.

propositions.text: CSW report shows state protection was available and claimants received adequate operational level protection.
propositions.quote: The evidence before this panel clearly indicates that the claimants received adequate state protection. This protection was at the operational level.

propositions.text: CSW report asked claimant and children to seek police protection and inform CSW about repeated violence.
propositions.quote: the CSW report asks that the claimant and her children be encouraged to seek protection from the police and inform the CSW regarding repeated violence by XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the CSW report shows state protection was available and claimants received adequate operational protection.

propositions.text: In 2011, claimant's ex-husband assaulted claimant; they were divorced but living in common-law relationship.
propositions.quote: on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 the claimant's ex-husband, by now the couple was divorced, but were living in a common-law relationship had physically and verbally assaulted the claimant.

propositions.text: Incident was reported; ex-husband arrested, charged, pled guilty, sentenced to 90 days imprisonment.
propositions.quote: he was arrested and charged, as he should have been. The panel notes that he was brought before the court on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. He pled guilty and was sentenced to 90 days imprisonment.

propositions.text: No reliable evidence that authorities failed to provide adequate protection or that ex-husband breached protection order.
propositions.quote: Therefore, there is no reliable evidence before this panel that the authorities did not provide the claimant and her children with adequate protection.

propositions.text: Claimant's allegation that police ignored breaches of protection order appears fabricated; protection order had expired and claimant and ex-husband resumed living together.
propositions.quote: there is no reliable evidence before this panel that the claimant's husband breached any protection order, which she allegedly reported and about which the police did nothing. This appears to have been concocted by the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds ex-husband assaulted claimant, was arrested and sentenced; no evidence police failed protection or breaches occurred; claimant fabricated breaches claim.

propositions.text: Court report states ex-husband still lives with claimant in common-law union after divorce.
propositions.quote: the court report states that Mr. XXXX "still resides with the claimant in a common-law union although they were married to one another before and divorced each other".

propositions.text: No reliable evidence ex-husband breached restraining order; claimant admitted he returned after order expired.
propositions.quote: There is no reliable evidence that Mr. XXXX, at any time, had breached any restraining order. The claimant herself testified that as soon as the restraining order had expired "he was back with us".

propositions.text: Claimant fabricated story that ex-husband routinely violated court orders and police failed to act; done to bolster refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant made up the story that her counsel so eloquently echoed that "her former spouse routinely violated Court orders which imposed no-contact provisions" and that the "police failed to act to enforce the Court Orders or charge her former spouse upon breaches, although Ms. XXXX reported the breaches to the police".

propositions.text: No state can guarantee perfect protection.
propositions.quote: The panel reminds itself that no state can guarantee perfect protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence ex-husband breached restraining order; claimant fabricated breach claims to bolster refugee status; no state guarantees perfect protection.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges ex-husband raped her daughter and tried to rape another daughter.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that her ex-husband raped her daughter from her first marriage and subsequently tried to rape one of his own daughters.

propositions.text: Claimant's contradictory testimony about reporting and police action undermines credibility of rape allegation.
propositions.quote: Given that the claimant just testified that she believed that the court case in the matter was proceeding, but now she said that the police will not do anything about it, she was asked to explain the contradiction.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant alleges ex-husband raped daughters but finds her contradictory testimony undermines credibility of rape allegation.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation about rape report is unreasonable and undermines credibility of daughter's rape claim.
propositions.quote: The panel finds her explanation unreasonable which undermines the claimant's credibility that her daughter was raped by her ex-husband.

propositions.text: Ex-husband sentenced to 75 days prison; court document confirms sentence effective 2010.
propositions.quote: In addition, her ex-husband was sentenced to 75 days in prison. The court document for the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 incident stated that the claimant's ex-husband's sentence for the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 incident became effective on XXXX XXXX, 2010.

propositions.text: Claimant testified ex-husband jailed 15 days and removed from home for 3 months; panel doubts 15 days claim.
propositions.quote: She also testified that her ex-husband was in jail for only 15 days. Even if that was the case (and the panel does not believe it because the court document said he was sentenced to 75 days), he was ordered removed from his home for three months.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence ex-husband breached restraining order; he returned home after order expired.
propositions.quote: there is no persuasive evidence that he breached his restraining order. The claimant testified that her ex-husband would come home as soon as the restraining order expired.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe ex-husband attempted to rape daughter; claimant was physically assaulted twice and authorities dealt adequately.
propositions.quote: Given the credibility problems with the claimant the panel does not believe that her ex-husband attempted to rape his daughter, XXXX. The panel believes that the claimant was physically assaulted twice, which the authorities dealt with adequately.

propositions.text: Panel finds no physical assault before 2010 by ex-husband.
propositions.quote: the panel does not believe that she was ever physically assaulted before 2010 by her husband.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's rape allegation lacks credibility; ex-husband sentenced; no evidence of restraining order breach; claimant assaulted twice and protected.

propositions.text: Sheikh case allows general credibility finding to extend to all relevant claimant testimony evidence.
propositions.quote: ... even without disbelieving every word [a claimant] has uttered, a...panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim...

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Sheikh case allowing general credibility findings to negate all claimant testimony evidence relevant to claim.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows domestic violence remains a problem in Croatia with some government and NGO efforts to address it.
propositions.quote: Croatia demonstrates that in regards to the documentary evidence, violence against women, including spousal abuse, remained a problem... The government has made evident strides in its efforts to prevent, respond to and punish domestic violence since its initial adoption of the LPDV.

propositions.text: In 2011, 11 women killed from domestic violence, 22% of all murders; courts imposed only 50% of protective measures.
propositions.quote: In 2011, 11 women were killed as a result of domestic violence, representing 22 percent of all murders in the country. The ombudswoman for gender equality reported that courts imposed only 50 percent of available protective measures...

propositions.text: Government finances most services; NGOs run shelters but funding is insufficient and irregular; 17 shelters exist.
propositions.quote: Although the government financed most services, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) oversaw shelters and claimed that funding was insufficient and irregular. NGOs and local governments operated 17 shelters.

propositions.text: Croatian government adopted Law on Protection against Domestic Violence in 2003 with protective measures and offender treatments.
propositions.quote: In 2003, the Croatian government adopted the Law on Protection against Domestic Violence (LPDV)... provides both urgent (emergency) and long-term protective measures...

propositions.text: Law allows police to file for protective measures; violations punishable by fine or imprisonment.
propositions.quote: most often, police file for these measures on behalf of victims... A violation of the protective measure is punishable by a fine or imprisonment of at least ten days.

propositions.text: Government amended laws and issued protocols to improve implementation of domestic violence protections.
propositions.quote: The government has amended the LDPV (2009) and promulgated regulations to further implementation of this law...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds domestic violence remains a problem in Croatia but government and NGOs have made evident efforts and legal improvements.

propositions.text: Civil society organizations actively support domestic violence victims with shelters, counseling, and specialized services.
propositions.quote: there are 32 organisations in the country actively providing support and assistance to victims of violence. Of those, 12 offer shelter services, 18 offer counselling services, one works as a centre for victims of sexual violence, and one offers counselling over the phone.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes civil society organizations provide various support services to domestic violence victims in Croatia.

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded state agencies in Croatia fail to provide adequate protection to people like claimant currently.
propositions.quote: the panel is not persuaded that, at this time, state agencies in Croatia are not making serious efforts to provide adequate protection to people like the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Croatia's state agencies currently make serious efforts to provide adequate protection to people like the claimant.

propositions.text: Croatian authorities have addressed domestic abuse and continue to do so; adequate operational protection exists despite imperfections.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that Croatian authorities have addressed and appear to continue to address domestic abuse within Croatian society... there is adequate state protection at the operational level for its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Croatian authorities address domestic abuse and provide adequate operational protection despite imperfections.

propositions.text: Estimated 30,000-40,000 Roma in Croatia face open discrimination and harassment despite constitutional protections.
propositions.quote: Documentary evidence indicates that there an estimated 30,000 and 40,000 Roma in Croatia and that while constitutional protections against discrimination applied to all minorities, open discrimination and harassment... continued against ethnic Serbs and Roma.

propositions.text: Negative majority attitudes hinder minority inclusion and sustainable return.
propositions.quote: Negative attitudes of much of the majority population are a serious obstacle to sustainable return and inclusion of minorities in all aspects of society.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Roma in Croatia face open discrimination and societal hostility despite constitutional protections.

propositions.text: State makes serious efforts and shows progress in minority protection despite patchy implementation due to political will.
propositions.quote: While some are critical stating that efforts are insufficient, the state is making serious efforts and there are signs of progress... implementation, however, has been patchy, often due to lacking political will.

propositions.text: Ethnic minorities guaranteed parliamentary representation and programs exist to address Roma exclusion.
propositions.quote: Ethnic minority groups including Serbs and Roma among others are guaranteed a minimum of eight representatives in the parliament and there are a number of programs to address Roma exclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Croatia makes serious efforts and progress in minority protection despite patchy implementation and guarantees parliamentary representation.

propositions.text: Only 6.5% of Roma have permanent jobs; over 90% live on social aid; government spending on Roma programs increased.
propositions.quote: It is estimated that only 6.5 percent of Roma had permanent jobs, while the government estimated more than 90 percent of registered Roma lived on social aid... Government spending on programs for Roma increased from 17 million kunas ($3 million) in 2008 to 27 million kunas in 2009 ($4.8 million).

propositions.text: Minority situation improved over 10 years; harassment and discrimination remain but ethnic relations stable.
propositions.quote: The situation of minorities in Croatia has improved in the last 10 years, and while members of minorities are still confronted by harassment and discrimination, the overall ethnic and religious relations remained stable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Roma face economic hardship but government spending increased; minority situation improved though discrimination persists.

propositions.text: Education is free and compulsory through grade eight; Romani children face obstacles including discrimination and lack of family support.
propositions.quote: Documentary evidence indicates that education is free and compulsory through grade eight... Romani children faced serious obstacles in continuing their education, including discrimination in schools and a lack of family support.

propositions.text: Romani preschool enrollment slightly decreased in 2009-10 but new Romani student numbers increased.
propositions.quote: The number of Romani children enrolled in preschool education for the 2009-10 school year was 588, a slight decrease from 595 in 2008... the number of new Romani students increased to 4,186 from 3,940 in 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds education is free and compulsory; Romani children face discrimination and obstacles; preschool enrollment slightly decreased but new students increased.

propositions.text: State reimburses kindergarten fees and provides scholarships to Romani students in high school and university.
propositions.quote: The state continued and expanded reimbursement of kindergarten fees to Romani parents... there were 350 scholarships to Romani students in high school... The number of Romani students receiving scholarships for university-level studies increased to 26 from 20.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the state provides financial support to Romani students through fee reimbursements and scholarships.

propositions.text: State aware of Roma education obstacles and programs show some success despite ongoing discrimination in Roma-only classes.
propositions.quote: It is clear that the state is aware of the obstacles faced by Roma students and have taken steps to help... The growth of the programs would also indicate that the programs are reaching more Roma students; a sign of some success.

propositions.text: ECHR ruled state discriminated against Roma students in Roma-only classes but previous ruling cleared state; state amended law to provide language classes.
propositions.quote: The ECHR Grand Chamber ruled that the state had discriminated against 13 Romani students... just a few months after the ruling the state amended the Law on Primary and Secondary Education to provide additional language classes to children who do not speak Croatian.

propositions.text: ECHR rulings on Roma-only classes show issues are not always clear discrimination or persecution.
propositions.quote: The flip-flop of the ECHR gives some indication that the issues around Roma only classes are not always clear cut discrimination, much less persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds state programs help Roma students despite discrimination; ECHR rulings on Roma-only classes are mixed and state amended law accordingly.

propositions.text: Complaints exist about slow or ineffective authority response to discrimination, intimidation, or violence against minorities.
propositions.quote: there are complaints that there is a slow or ineffective reaction by authorities to discrimination, intimidation or violence towards members of minorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes complaints about slow or ineffective authority responses to minority discrimination and violence.

propositions.text: In September, ethnic Croat parents blocked Romani children from attending class citing overcrowding and hygiene; police intervened and compromise reached.
propositions.quote: On September 17, approximately 50 ethnic Croat parents prevented 44 Romani children from attending class... Police intervened to prevent the situation from escalating, and local officials brokered a compromise to allow the Romani preschoolers to attend classes.

propositions.text: President Josipovic condemned the effort to prevent Romani children attending preschool as unacceptable and discriminatory.
propositions.quote: President Josipovic stated that the effort to prevent ethnic Romani children from attending the preschool was particularly unacceptable and discriminatory.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds ethnic Croat parents blocked Romani children from school; police intervened; president condemned the discrimination.

propositions.text: New ombudsman law enacted to strengthen human rights protection and coordinate with civil society; merger delayed pending new appointment.
propositions.quote: On July 10, parliament enacted a new ombudsman law to strengthen the institution's ability to protect human rights... By year's end, however, the merger did not take place as the government sought to first appoint a new ombudsperson.

propositions.text: Ombudsman authorized to initiate shortened procedures and disciplinary proceedings but did not exercise authority during year.
propositions.quote: The ombudsman now has the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings against institutions that fail to respond to his interventions. The ombudsman did not exercise this authority during the year.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds new ombudsman law strengthens human rights protection but merger delayed; ombudsman did not use new disciplinary powers yet.

propositions.text: Croatia is a functioning democracy with free elections, civilian-controlled security forces, no reports of unlawful killings or disappearances, and free criticism of government.
propositions.quote: Croatia is a functioning democracy, although needing improvement in some areas. There are free and fair elections... security forces reported to civilian authorities... no reports the government or its agents committed arbitrary or unlawful killings... individuals may freely criticize the government publicly or privately without reprisal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Croatia is a functioning democracy with free elections, civilian security control, no unlawful killings, and free government criticism.

propositions.text: Law provides criminal penalties for official corruption but government did not always implement laws effectively; corruption remained serious problem
propositions.quote: the law provides criminal penalties for official corruption the government did not always implement the laws effectively, and corruption remained a serious problem

propositions.text: Large backlogs of unresolved criminal and civil cases exist
propositions.quote: there are large backlogs of unresolved criminal and civil cases

propositions.text: Prosecution of some domestic war crimes trials is ineffective
propositions.quote: ineffective prosecution of some domestic war crimes trials

propositions.text: Lack of progress in restoring nationalized property to Serb Orthodox Church and Coordination of Jewish Communities in Croatia
propositions.quote: a lack of progress in restoring nationalized property to the Serb Orthodox Church and Coordination of Jewish Communities in Croatia

propositions.text: Incidents of societal violence and discrimination against ethnic minorities and due to sexual orientation occur
propositions.quote: incidents of societal violence and discrimination against ethnic minorities and due to sexual orientation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds corruption remains serious, backlogs exist, prosecutions ineffective, property restoration lacking, and societal violence and discrimination occur.

propositions.text: Croatia is not in a state of collapse and has a structured, functioning police service
propositions.quote: Croatia is not in a state of collapse. Croatia has a structured and functioning police service

propositions.text: National police have primary responsibility for national security; military may be called in times of disorder
propositions.quote: The national police have primary responsibility for national security; in times of disorder, the prime minister and the president may call upon the military to provide security

propositions.text: Police obtain arrest warrants by presenting probable cause to investigative magistrate and justify arrests within 24 hours
propositions.quote: Police obtained arrest warrants by presenting probable cause to an investigative magistrate. The police have 24 hours to justify an arrest to a magistrate

propositions.text: Police must provide arrested persons access to attorney within 24 hours
propositions.quote: Police must provide those arrested with access to an attorney of their choice within 24 hours

propositions.text: Constitution and law provide for independent judiciary, generally respected by government
propositions.quote: The constitution and law provide for an independent judiciary, and the government generally respected judicial independence

propositions.text: As of Dec 31, 2011, prisons held 5,084 offenders, exceeding system capacity of 3,921 prisoners
propositions.quote: As of December 31, 2011, prisons and youth detention facilities held 5,084 offenders, although the system's capacity was 3,921 prisoners

propositions.text: Police service investigates crime including against minorities, though prosecutions of race crimes are not always pursued
propositions.quote: This indicates that the police service will investigate crime, even crime against minorities, although as noted above, prosecutions of race crimes are not always prosecuted

propositions.text: State protection is not perfect
propositions.quote: The protection of the state is not perfect

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Croatia's police and judiciary function with some imperfections, including overcrowded prisons and imperfect state protection.

propositions.text: Claimants are Roma and victims of domestic violence who received help from authorities
propositions.quote: The claimants are Roma and as victims of domestic violence, when they approached the authorities for help, they were given help

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence claimant would not receive help in future if needed
propositions.quote: There is no persuasive evidence before this panel that they would not receive help in the future should they require it

propositions.text: Claimant has not provided clear and convincing evidence that state protection in Croatia is inadequate
propositions.quote: the claimant has not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Croatia is inadequate

propositions.text: If claimants return to Croatia, they could reasonably expect adequate state protection
propositions.quote: if the claimants return to Croatia, they could reasonably expect the state to be forthcoming with serious efforts at adequate protection

propositions.text: Documentary evidence on protection for Roma is mixed but claimant failed to show failure of state protection
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence with respect to protection for the Roma in Croatia is mixed but the claimants have not provided clear and convincing evidence of a failure of state protection

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants received help as Roma domestic violence victims and failed to prove inadequate state protection in Croatia.

propositions.text: Claimant has not proven with clear and convincing evidence that state protection would be unavailable if she returned and faced issues with former spouse
propositions.quote: the claimant has not discharged the burden of proving with clear and convincing evidence that state protection in Croatia would not be available to her if she were to return to Croatia and face any issues with her former spouse

propositions.text: Country documentation supports domestic violence remains a problem in Croatia
propositions.quote: the country documentation does support that domestic violence is still a problem in Croatia

propositions.text: Claimant received state protection in Croatia, even if imperfect
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant received state protection while she was in Croatia even if it was not perfect

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to prove lack of state protection despite domestic violence issues; she received protection in Croatia.

propositions.text: Claimant has not rebutted presumption of adequate state protection
propositions.quote: claimant has not rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection

propositions.text: It is claimant's responsibility to provide clear and convincing evidence to rebut presumption of state protection
propositions.quote: it is the responsibility of the claimant to provide such evidence to rebut the presumption

propositions.text: Adequate state protection is available to claimant in Croatia
propositions.quote: there is adequate state protection available to the claimant in Croatia

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to rebut presumption of adequate state protection, which is her burden, and that protection is available in Croatia.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and, as the issue of state protection is applicable to both sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA, her claim must fail

propositions.text: Other claimants relying on her claim have also failed
propositions.quote: the panel finds the other claimants whose claim also rests on her claim have failed as well

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant and others relying on her claim failed to rebut state protection presumption; claim must fail under IRPA.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; claim rejected
propositions.quote: The panel concludes that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection and rejects her claim

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not a refugee or protected person and rejects her claim.
